simple: This page is about `LinearVelocity`, a constraint that keeps a part moving at a steady speed in a direction you choose. Physics pushes the part harder or softer as needed so the speed stays the same. It is great for things like conveyor belts, moving platforms, or a hovercraft that cruises forward. You can also choose whether the direction follows the world or follows the part as it turns.
analogy: It is like cruise control in a car: you pick a speed, and the car gives more or less gas by itself to stay at that speed, even going uphill.
keyPoints: `LinearVelocity` applies force to an assembly so it keeps a constant velocity (speed plus direction).
It can control speed along a full 3D direction (a `Vector3`), along one line, or across a flat 2D plane.
If you want to choose how much push is used instead of what speed to reach, use `VectorForce` instead.
If you only need a starting push (like a launch), set the part's `AssemblyLinearVelocity` once instead of using a constraint.
The `RelativeTo` property decides what the direction is measured against: `World` or one of the two attachments.
With `RelativeTo` set to `World`, a velocity of (0, 0, 10) always means 10 studs per second along the world Z axis, no matter which way the part faces.
With `RelativeTo` set to `Attachment0`, the direction turns with the attachment, so 'forward' stays the part's own forward.

terms.constraint: An object that controls how parts move, like an invisible motor, rope, or hand pushing them. Mover constraints push or spin parts for you.
terms.assembly: A group of parts that are welded or joined together so physics moves them as one piece. A car body plus its welded seats is one assembly.
terms.attachment: A small invisible point you put inside a part. Constraints hook onto attachments, the same way a rope ties onto a hook.
terms.Attachment0 / Attachment1: The two attachment slots a constraint uses. Attachment0 is usually the one that gets pushed; Attachment1 is the other end or the reference point.
terms.velocity: Speed plus a direction. A velocity of (0, 0, 10) means moving 10 studs every second along the Z axis.
terms.constant velocity: A speed and direction that stay the same over time instead of speeding up or slowing down.
terms.Vector3: Three numbers (X, Y, Z) that describe a direction or position in 3D. (0, 10, 0) points straight up with a size of 10.
terms.2D plane: A flat surface, like a tabletop. Moving 'in a plane' means sliding in two directions but not the third.
terms.relative to World: Directions are measured using the fixed world axes, which never turn. Up is always up, no matter how the part spins.
terms.relative to an attachment: Directions are measured from the attachment's own facing. If the attachment turns 90 degrees, its 'forward' turns 90 degrees too.
terms.studs per second: How Roblox measures speed. 10 studs per second means the part travels 10 studs every second.

example.title: Make a block slide forward at a steady speed
example.place: Script inside a Part in Workspace (make sure the part is not Anchored)
example.code:
local part = script.Parent

-- The constraint needs an attachment inside the part to push on
local attachment = Instance.new("Attachment")
attachment.Parent = part

local linearVelocity = Instance.new("LinearVelocity")
linearVelocity.Attachment0 = attachment
linearVelocity.RelativeTo = Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo.World
linearVelocity.VelocityConstraintMode = Enum.VelocityConstraintMode.Vector
linearVelocity.VectorVelocity = Vector3.new(0, 0, 10) -- 10 studs per second along world Z
linearVelocity.MaxForce = math.huge -- allow as much force as needed
linearVelocity.Parent = part
explain: We grab the part the script lives in.
We make an `Attachment` inside it, because constraints push on attachments.
We create a `LinearVelocity` and hook it to that attachment with `Attachment0`.
`RelativeTo = World` means the direction (0, 0, 10) uses the world's axes, not the part's.
`MaxForce = math.huge` lets the constraint push as hard as it needs to keep the speed.
Parenting the constraint to the part turns it on, and the block starts gliding.

watchOut: Anchored parts do not move with physics. Turn off `Anchored` or nothing will happen.
Forgetting to set `Attachment0` means the constraint has nothing to push, so it does nothing.
If `MaxForce` is too small for a heavy part, it may never reach the speed you asked for. Raise `MaxForce`.
Do not use `LinearVelocity` for a one-time launch; it keeps pushing forever. Set `AssemblyLinearVelocity` once instead.
